plan.contextChunk: This figure contains two panels illustrating depth of field in a lens system. Top panel: a geometric diagram showing the variables used to compute depth of field, including the lens, the object and sensor planes, circle of confusion C, aperture f/N, and object distance U, with objects at different depths focusing at different positions relative to the sensor. Bottom panel: a second ray diagram with a narrowed aperture (marked in red), annotated 'larger depth of field', showing geometrically how stopping down the aperture extends the in-focus range. The figure introduces the geometric optics of focus and blur as foundational concepts in lens-based imaging.

interactionPlan.concept: For the same focused object distance, narrowing the aperture makes the acceptable-focus range larger because defocused ray cones make smaller blur circles at the image plane.

authoredContext:
Objects closer or further from the focal plane will come into focus
behind or in front of the sensor plane, respectively, resulting in a
blur circle at the sensor plane, as illustrated in
figures -circleOfConfusion and -DOFformula.

Circle of confusion and depth of field. (Top) Variables used in the computation of the depth of field of a lens. (Bottom) The elongation of the depth of field size for a given tolerable circle of confusion results from narrowing the lens aperture . The catch is that narrowing the aperture results in less light reaching the sensor plane.

When the circle of
confusion, $C$, is much smaller than the lens aperture, $f/N$, then the
term $N^2 C^2 D^2$ can be ignored relative to $f^4$, and we have
$$D \approx \frac{2 N C U^2}{f^2}$$ Note that for smaller camera
f-numbers, $N$ (larger apertures), the depth of field decreases in
proportion. This effect can be seen in the bottom of -DOFformula, and in -rulers.

plan.concept: Depth of field is the range of object distances that produce an acceptably small circle of confusion on the sensor, and it grows when the aperture is narrowed or the focus distance changes.

interactions.label: Aperture f-number N
interactions.teaches: Increasing the f-number narrows the aperture, narrows the ray cone, reduces blur for the same defocus, and therefore expands the depth-of-field interval

interactions.label: Focus object distance U
interactions.teaches: Changing the focused object distance shifts the near and far acceptable-focus limits rather than simply translating a fixed depth-of-field bracket

demo_steps.title: Wide aperture, shallow depth of field
demo_steps.narration: With a low f-number, the aperture is wide and the ray cone is steep. Points slightly in front of or behind the focused object distance form a large circle of confusion, so the acceptable depth range is short.

demo_steps.title: Stop down the lens
demo_steps.narration: Increasing the f-number narrows the aperture. The same defocused object points now make smaller blur circles on the sensor, so the near and far depth-of-field limits move farther apart.

demo_steps.title: Refocus farther away
demo_steps.narration: Moving the focused object plane farther from the lens shifts the geometry of the ray bundles. The depth-of-field limits move with the focus distance, and the far limit expands differently from the near limit.

plan.keyInsight: Stopping down the aperture increases depth of field because a narrower ray cone makes out-of-focus points blur less on the sensor.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Use a clean 2D geometric optics layout with object space on the left, lens in the middle-right, and sensor plane on the far right. Preserve the textbook visual language: blue vertical lens plane, red object and sensor planes, black lens/aperture shape, thick blue main ray bundles, thinner pale-blue auxiliary rays, dotted black construction lines, and serif italic math labels. The aperture slider should visibly change the vertical opening at the lens and the angle of the rays; the depth-of-field bracket on the object side should lengthen as N increases. The object-distance slider should move the focused object plane and update U, D1, D2, ray intersections, and the circle-of-confusion size consistently. Replace the original two stacked static panels with one dynamic diagram plus a red 'larger depth of field' annotation that becomes prominent as the aperture narrows.
